content_voiceover: This is the drug and chemical list for G6PD deficiency, and you don't need to memorize every entry, you need to recognize the pattern and a few named agents. These are all oxidant stressors, unsafe for WHO class I, II, and III variants because those patients can't regenerate reduced glutathione fast enough to buffer the oxidative load. The classic named agents worth knowing are primaquine, the antimalarial that's a textbook trigger question, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, sulfa drugs like sulfacetamide, sulfanilamide, and sulfapyridine, and of course fava beans, which give you favism, most severe in the Mediterranean and Kaiping variants. The one highlighted in red here, and clinically the most important for an inpatient hematology consult, is urate oxidase, rasburicase, used for tumor lysis syndrome. Giving rasburicase to a G6PD deficient patient can trigger severe, even fatal, hemolysis, so screening G6PD status before starting rasburicase is standard practice, especially in patients of African, Mediterranean, or Asian descent. On the safe side, acetaminophen, aspirin, and ascorbic acid are fine to use.
keypoints: Classic oxidant triggers: primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, fava beans
Rasburicase (urate oxidase) — screen G6PD before giving for tumor lysis syndrome
Rasburicase-induced hemolysis can be severe/fatal in deficient patients
keypoint_voiceover: The high-yield drug list boils down to a few names. Primaquine, dapsone, sulfa drugs, nitrofurantoin, and fava beans are classic oxidant triggers you should recognize instantly.
